draft.body:
Block, the financial technology parent company of Square and Cash App led by Jack Dorsey, announced an experimental AI voice model named Dessa on October 23, 2026. Built by an in-house deep learning lab, Dessa is a full-duplex speech-to-speech conversational model that the company states was trained from scratch entirely on spoken audio without using written text datasets or pre-trained language models.

According to [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1017906/jack-dorsey-block-dessa-ai-voice-speech), the project aims to bypass the text bottlenecks standard in conventional voice agents. Most commercial voice assistants process human speech by converting incoming audio into text transcripts, running that text through a traditional large language model, and then feeding the generated text into a synthetic speech synthesizer. Block claims Dessa processes and outputs raw audio directly, allowing it to perceive acoustic nuances such as sarcasm, emotional distress, sighs, and spontaneous laughter.

## Audio-First Architecture Without Text Pipelines

In its documentation, Block states that human infants learn spoken language long before they encounter written text, inspiring the research team to investigate whether a neural network could do the same. According to Block's research page, typical text-to-speech and automatic speech recognition pipelines discard non-verbal acoustic signals like cadence, intonation, and stress placement. Block claims that by abandoning text intermediaries, Dessa handles conversational timing natively.

The system operates using a full-duplex architecture, meaning the agent can listen while it speaks. Traditional voice models frequently suffer from awkward conversational collisions, either cutting off abruptly or failing to register interruptions until a spoken phrase finishes. Block says Dessa learned when to yield the floor, when to interject, and when to produce backchannel verbal cues—such as brief affirmations—to indicate it is actively following a speaker's thoughts.

Unlike systems from ElevenLabs or Fish Audio that rely on synthetic tags to introduce emotional styling, Block claims Dessa's emotional responsiveness emerges directly from its training data, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/24/blocks-new-voice-model-sounds-eerily-human/). According to Block, the model learned language from hundreds of times fewer words than traditional large language models, though speech audio data is far denser per word than pure text files.

[[FIG1]]

## Local Execution and Training on NVIDIA GB200 Hardware

Block's research team trained Dessa using a single NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack system, according to [Unite.AI](https://www.unite.ai/block-unveils-dessa-a-full-duplex-speech-model-trained-on-conversation/). Despite the compute demands associated with continuous audio token processing, Block reported that inference runs faster than real time on consumer-grade hardware.

The company confirmed that Dessa can execute fully on-device on an Apple MacBook Pro equipped with an M4 Max chip or better. This allows the system to run on-device.

Block's AI research lab was founded by former members of the Toronto deep learning startup Dessa and is led by Ragavan Thurairatnam, who previously founded and sold Dessa. The research roster credited on the project includes Louay Hazami, Hashiam Kadhim, Qi Liu, Rayhane Mama, Aydin Polat, and Marc Tyndel, alongside several student interns. The lab reports directly to Dorsey, who serves as Block's head and chairman.

[[FIG2]]

## Live Voice Demos Show Pauses, Laughs, and Uncanny Nuance

Accompanying the announcement, Block released several unscripted audio recordings highlighting Dessa's conversational flow. In one demonstration shared by Thurairatnam, a speaker conversed casually with the agent, which responded with colloquial phrasing, acknowledged feeling tired from manual labor, and referenced fictional family details with the cadence of an African American man, as noted by [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/check-out-the-many-uncanny-human-ish-voices-from-blocks-new-ai-model-2000830237).

Other published clips demonstrated spontaneous reactions. When an interlocutor asked about a surprise anniversary, Dessa responded with audible gasps, whereas a prompt about a surprise trip to Paris was described as eliciting teary gratitude. In another clip detailed by [Mashable](https://mashable.com/tech/block-unveils-new-ai-model-dessa-trained-entirely-on-human-speech), Dessa held a discussion regarding Christopher Nolan's filmography and naturally supplied a movie title, while laughing mid-sentence was listed separately by Block as a distinct demonstration highlight.

The demonstrations also exposed rough edges. During an interactive guessing game with a lab intern, Dessa correctly identified items on the first try but failed to recognize the game was over, continuing to guess even after being told it had already won. In another demo, the model mistakenly addressed a speaker as "Ronaldo." Block also published a comparison clip pitting Dessa against an AI voice model from OpenAI, arguing that Dessa's natural interruptions sounded more conversational than traditional speech synthesizers.

## Safety Testing, Research Waitlist, and Enterprise Implications

Block has not made Dessa publicly accessible. Instead, the company published an intake form granting closed early access to AI safety researchers, asking for an institutional email from a university, company, or lab.

In its release statement, Block framed the speech-first approach as an important safety consideration, arguing that current voice systems remain functionally deaf to physical pain or urgency in a user's voice because text transcriptions erase emotional context. However, researchers may test whether the model could trick people on the other end.

While Dessa originated as an exploratory research effort, the technology holds direct practical relevance for Block's broader business footprint. The company's Square division already uses voice AI to handle ordering. Running the model on-device could power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.

faq.q: What makes Block's Dessa different from traditional voice assistants?
faq.a: Traditional voice systems transcribe spoken audio into text, process that text with a language model, and convert the output back into synthesized speech. According to Block, Dessa is a direct speech-to-speech model trained entirely on human conversation without any text data, allowing it to process emotional inflections, laughter, and vocal cadence directly.

faq.q: What hardware is required to run Dessa locally?
faq.a: Block states that Dessa can run locally on an Apple MacBook Pro with an M4 Max processor or higher, allowing real-time, on-device audio inference without relying on cloud servers.

faq.q: Is Dessa publicly available to download or test?
faq.a: No. Block has not released Dessa publicly. The company has made early access available exclusively to vetted AI safety researchers via an application form, alongside a general public waitlist.
